title: Noam Brown, Ilge Akkaya & Hunter Lightman of OpenAI's o1 Research Team on Teaching LLMs to Reason Better by Thinking Longer
pub: Sequoia Capital, 'Training Data' podcast (hosts Sonya Huang and Pat Grady)
author: Noam Brown · Ilge Akkaya · Hunter Lightman · Sonya Huang · Pat Grady

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that capability is task-specific and does not establish general competence or wholesale human replacement. It reports gains on verifiable STEM tasks while stressing benchmark-selection limits, engineering constraints, diminishing returns and uncertainty about broader performance. It does not materially address legal workflow redesign, user expertise or professional verification practices.
qs: **Noam Brown:** I mentioned before that there’s some tasks that are like reasoning tasks that are easier to verify than they are to generate a solution for, and there’s some tasks that don’t really fall into that category.
**Hunter Lightman:** I don’t think we’re quite at that level yet.

kp.k: Reinforcement learning enables general inference-time reasoning
kp.d: Ilge Akkaya describes o1 as trained through reinforcement learning to think, with reported generalisation across reasoning domains. Noam Brown contrasts this with domain-specific gameplay reasoning methods, such as Monte Carlo tree search in Go. These are researchers’ accounts of their own system, not independently established findings presented in the transcript.
qs: So the o1 model series are trained with RL to be able to think, and you could call it reasoning, maybe also.
The way that it’s thinking for longer is actually quite general and can be used for a lot of different domains.

kp.k: Reasoning gains depend on the problem’s structure
kp.d: Brown offers a non-canonical definition of reasoning: problems benefiting from additional time to consider alternatives. His generator–verifier gap distinguishes tasks such as Sudoku, where recognising a solution is easier than generating one, from factual recall, where additional thinking may not help. He uses this distinction to explain o1’s reported STEM gains; verification here means recognising solution correctness, not human review of professional AI output.
qs: I’m not claiming that this is the canonical one.
You might call it, like, a generator verifier gap, where it’s really hard to generate a correct solution, but it’s much easier to recognize when you have one.
And I think STEM problems tend to fall into the, like, what we would consider hard reasoning problems.

kp.k: Longer thinking reportedly produces backtracking and self-correction
kp.d: Hunter Lightman identifies an internal breakthrough when an o1 training run exceeded earlier bespoke systems on unspecified mathematics evaluations and displayed backtracking. Brown reports that allowing longer thinking produced mistake recognition and alternative approaches almost emergently. The transcript supplies neither evaluation scores nor experimental controls for these observations.
qs: it was scoring higher on the math evals than any of our other attempts, any of our bespoke systems.
And we called this backtracking.
And we saw that once it’s able to think for longer, it develops these abilities almost emergently that were very powerful and contain things like backtracking and self correction

kp.k: Deep reinforcement learning complements rather than replaces pretraining
kp.d: Brown recounts deep RL enthusiasm around 2015–2018 and 2019, followed by disillusionment as large language models succeeded without it. He argues that earlier attention to learning from scratch underappreciated learning from human data, including its contribution to AlphaGo. He presents o1 as evidence that RL becomes powerful in combination with other elements, while forecasting broader impact rather than documenting that impact.
qs: I remember what it was like in, like, you know, 2015 to 2018, 2019, and deep RL was the hot thing.
But I think partly because of this focus on learning from scratch, this GPT paradigm kind of flew under the radar for a while
And what we’re seeing now with o1 is that actually there is a place for it, and it can be quite powerful when it’s combined with these other elements as well.

kp.k: Competition performance reveals uneven, sometimes unconventional problem-solving
kp.d: Lightman describes an anecdotal programming solution that used an unusual method, explicitly declining to call it genius. He reports that o1 earned half credit on one IOI problem humans found difficult but struggled on another humans handled well. The comparison supports his account of differing capability profiles, not general superiority over human programmers.
qs: I don’t think it was quite a, like, this is a stroke of genius moment.

For the actual IOI competition, there was one problem that humans did really poor on that the model was able to get half credit on, and then another problem that humans did really well on that the model was, like, barely able to get off the ground on.

kp.k: Scientific brainstorming illustrates assistance rather than autonomous research
kp.d: Akkaya reports seeing physicians and researchers describe using o1 to brainstorm cancer research, gene discovery and gene therapy directions. This is an account of user reports, not evidence of completed discoveries or validated research outcomes. She explicitly characterises the model as a collaborator unable to conduct the research itself.
qs: I’ve seen a lot of MDs and researchers use the model as a brainstorming partner.
Clearly, the model cannot do the research itself, but it can just be a very nice collaborator with humans in this respect.

kp.k: Coding assistance does not establish whole-job substitution
kp.d: Responding to the host’s framing about interview performance and replacing engineers, Lightman says the system is not yet at that level. He reports that o1 feels like a better coding partner and has authored a couple of repository pull requests, but contrasts its few-minute reasoning episodes with his longer engineering work. Greater task coverage through scaling is presented as a possibility.
qs: I don’t think we’re quite at that level yet.
I think it’s already authored a couple of PRs in our repo
The thing that gives me pause is that the o1 is already better than me at math, but it’s not as good at me at being a software engineer.

kp.k: Benchmark results cannot establish general intelligence or occupational competence
kp.d: Lightman qualifies the host’s reported 120 IQ figure as performance on particular tests, not a cross-domain capability level. Brown similarly says outperforming many PhDs on GPQA does not imply superiority across their abilities. Both caution against extrapolating narrow benchmark results into general human equivalence.
qs: One of the important things is that it’s 120 IQ on some tests someone gave.
This doesn’t mean that it’s got like 120 IQ-level reasoning at all the different domains that we care about.
That doesn’t mean that it’s smarter than a PhD in every single way imaginable.
There’s a lot of things that a PhD can do that—you know, there’s a lot of things that a human can do, period, that the AI can’t do.

kp.k: Inference-time compute opens another scaling dimension
kp.d: Brown argues that o1’s significance lies partly in a relatively untapped scaling dimension beyond increasingly expensive pretraining and concerns about training-data availability. He predicts a higher capability ceiling, but the transcript does not provide numerical scaling laws or establish how far improvements will extend.
qs: There have been a lot of concerns that, like, AI might be hitting a wall or plateauing because pre-training is so expensive and becoming so expensive, and there’s all these questions around, like, is there enough data to train on.
The fact that we’re able to have this different dimension for scaling that is so far pretty untapped, I think is a big deal.
And I think it means that the ceiling is a lot higher than a lot of people have appreciated.

kp.k: Long-horizon improvements remain speculative and face diminishing returns
kp.d: Lightman hopes longer reasoning will improve already promising tasks, including mathematics research assistance, but is uncertain about currently weak domains and difficult unsolved theorems. Brown invokes exhaustive formal-proof search as a theoretical illustration of unlimited time, not a demonstrated o1 capability, and acknowledges diminishing returns. The discussion does not establish that all mathematical problems become practically solvable.
qs: We haven’t had o1 for years, so we haven’t been able to let it think that long yet.
Will it get better at the things that it’s not good at now?
we don’t know yet quite what the scaling of this is for how it relates to solving really hard math theorems.
it clearly gets in diminishing returns as you think for longer.

kp.k: Scaling requires engineering and better evaluation targets
kp.d: Brown compares inference-time scaling with the years of work needed to scale earlier GPT models. Lightman stresses large-scale systems engineering rather than merely having a simple research idea. Akkaya adds that researchers need to identify evaluation tasks on which additional test-time compute produces better outcomes, beyond existing standard benchmarks.
qs: it’s a simple idea, but there’s a lot of work that has to go into actually scaling it up.
And so there’s always a lot of just, like, hard engineering work to make these systems scale up.
So we do have these standard evals as benchmarks, but perhaps there are ones that we are not yet testing the model on.

kp.k: Deployment helps discover usefulness beyond researchers’ familiar domains
kp.d: Brown distinguishes raw model intelligence from practical usefulness and explains that releasing o1 preview was partly intended to discover applications and limitations. Lightman describes iterative deployment as a feedback mechanism, while Akkaya acknowledges researchers’ domain biases. The team does not supply a settled rule for choosing o1 over GPT-4; Lightman expressly acknowledges uneven performance.
qs: I think there’s clearly a gap between the raw intelligence of the model and how useful it is for various tasks.
It’s absolutely not better at everything.
One of the motivations that we had for releasing o1 preview is to see what people end up using it for and how they end up using it.
as researchers we are clearly biased towards the domains that we can understand.

kp.k: Smaller models trade capability costs against iteration speed
kp.d: Akkaya presents o1-mini and the heavier model as serving different purposes through a cheaper, faster versus slower trade-off. Lightman argues that faster iteration matters for research progress and hopes the smaller model will provide the same benefit to developers. No comparative prices, speeds or capability measurements are given.
qs: we are excited to have a cheaper, faster version and then kind of like a heavier, slower one as well.
o1-mini lets us iterate faster.
Hopefully, for the broader ecosystem of people playing with these models, o1 mini will also allow them to iterate faster.

kp.k: Readable reasoning traces remain withheld from users
kp.d: Lightman says the generated chains of thought are human-interpretable and useful for researchers inspecting model behaviour. Asked about withholding them, Brown says the decision was not contentious and compares risks of sharing the thinking process to releasing frontier-model weights. Competitive motives are introduced by the host as a description of OpenAI’s release blog, rather than independently elaborated by Brown here.
qs: these chains of thoughts the model produces are human interpretable
I don’t think it was contentious.
I think there’s a lot of risks to sharing the thinking process behind the model, and I think it’s a similar decision, actually.

kp.k: Economic task coverage frames AGI, but missing capabilities persist
kp.d: Brown identifies AGI rather than a specific application as OpenAI’s priority. Lightman offers a tentative economic conception based on the share of valuable jobs AI systems can perform, forecasting AI coworkers and changed work without a definite timeframe. He also leaves open whether strategic planning, ideation, creativity and organisational execution are all reasoning or require additional approaches.
qs: There’s no single, like, application that is the priority other than getting us to AGI.
I just think that it’s something about the proportion of economically valuable jobs that our models and our AI systems are able to do.
Is that reasoning, or is that a different kind of creativity that’s not quite reasoning and needs to be addressed differently?
And maybe eventually it’ll all look like reasoning to us, or maybe we’ll come up with a new word and there will be new steps we need to take to get there.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The researchers claim that inference-time reasoning improves problem-solving and could expand AI's contribution to research, software engineering and economically valuable work. This is a cross-domain source with no specific claim about legal services.
pts.d: Ilge Akkaya describes o1 as trained through reinforcement learning to think. Noam Brown claims that longer thinking generalizes across domains and produces backtracking and self-correction; he predicts that this additional scaling dimension raises AI's capability ceiling and that deep reinforcement learning could achieve impact comparable to GPT-4. Akkaya reports medical researchers using o1 to brainstorm research directions, explicitly as a collaborator rather than an autonomous researcher. Hunter Lightman describes o1 as a better coding partner than previous models and reports that it has authored repository pull requests; he tentatively predicts that longer reasoning will enable more software-engineering tasks. He also hopes it can become a useful assistant for novel mathematical research. More broadly, Lightman anticipates AI coworkers doing substantial parts of today's jobs while humans undertake different work. Akkaya and Lightman describe o1-mini's lower cost and greater speed as useful for faster iteration, with Lightman anticipating similar benefits for external developers and possible new products built on o1.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of researchers' first-hand observations, references to benchmarks and scaling results, internal coding experience, and anecdotal user reports; the broader work-transformation predictions are extrapolations.
pts.d: Lightman reports that an o1 training run exceeded their earlier bespoke systems on math evaluations, accompanied by observed backtracking in model outputs. He describes uneven performance relative to humans on individual IOI programming problems. Brown cites GPQA performance exceeding that of many PhDs, while explicitly denying that this demonstrates general superiority to PhDs. The interview refers to a published inference-time scaling trend but does not supply numerical scaling results or methods. Lightman's report of internally authored pull requests supports the narrower coding-assistance claim, not replacement of software engineers. Akkaya's medical-research examples are reports of uses she has seen, without controlled outcome evidence. Lightman's mathematical-research optimism draws partly on a professor's social-media report of a previously human-solved proof; this is second-hand anecdotal support, not evidence of a novel mathematical discovery. His AI-coworker forecast has no labour-market data or quantified displacement estimate attached.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current assistance claims concern the 2024 o1 release; larger capability and employment changes have no firm deadline and depend on scaling, engineering, task suitability and application development.
pts.d: The speakers distinguish current observations from hoped-for future progress. Lightman places wider work transformation over an unspecified number of years, not a dated forecast. Current reasoning runs last a few minutes, whereas software engineering requires longer and broader work. Brown's explanation emphasizes tasks where considering more options helps, particularly those where recognizing a correct solution is easier than generating it; this is a computational generation–checking distinction, not a claim about human verification of legal output. Lightman is more confident about improving tasks o1 already handles than about extending to weak domains. Brown acknowledges diminishing returns to longer thinking, and the speakers identify engineering and suitable evaluations as constraints. They do not establish that arbitrarily long inference yields general intelligence or solves all mathematical problems in practical time. They also distinguish benchmark performance from real-world usefulness and acknowledge that creativity, planning and organizational execution may require additional advances.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified beneficiaries and potentially affected workers are scientific researchers, mathematicians, software engineers, AI developers and, prospectively, workers performing economically valuable tasks.
pts.d: Akkaya identifies MDs and cancer researchers as users obtaining ideas for gene discovery and gene therapy research, while retaining responsibility for conducting the research. Lightman identifies mathematicians as prospective users of assistance with lemmas and proofs, and software engineers as current users of coding assistance with possible future expansion of task coverage. His comparison with his own engineering work explicitly preserves the distinction between solving competition problems and performing a whole job. OpenAI researchers benefit from faster iteration with o1-mini; external founders and developers may likewise iterate faster and build more capable applications. Lightman's wider AI-coworker scenario implies partial task substitution and changes in human work, but specifies neither occupations beyond these examples nor employment totals. The source does not identify effects on lawyers, law firms, legal clients or access to justice.
